_about: A complete, realistic response to the Purpose Playbook discovery questionnaire, keyed by
signalKey. It exists so the whole path — discovery flow, playbook agent, direction briefs,
the five specialists — can be exercised against answers a real client might give rather than
placeholder prose, which makes every derived field read 'not on record' and only proves the
The client is invented: Kindling Retrofit, a Bristol firm taking listed and historic buildings
off oil and gas. It was written to exercise the instrument's branching: three customer
segments, a buyer who is not the user, five competitor slots, three vision-board themes and an
existing logo, so every conditional block opens.
Values are the canonical option values where a question has options (what lands in the signal),
not the labels shown on screen. Keys absent from this file are questions a condition gates away.
Competitor and admired-brand URLs use example.com on purpose: nothing here should resolve to a
real business, since standing agents read client URLs for real.
setup.respondent: Rosa Pellew, founder and technical director
setup.oneLiner: We get old, protected buildings off oil and gas without wrecking what makes them worth protecting.
setup.sector: Low-carbon retrofit for historic and listed buildings
setup.teamSize: Eleven — six on site, three in design, two in the office
belief.origin: I spent nine years as a building services engineer on new-build schools, and every winter I'd get a call from a church warden or a bursar who had been quoted £400k for a heating system that would have cracked the plaster inside two seasons. The industry had one answer and it was designed for a new box. I started Kindling because somebody had to do the boring part properly: survey the fabric first, model the moisture, then size the plant. The first job was the Quaker meeting house on Redcliffe Hill. We took it off oil for a third of what the national contractor had quoted, and the 1740 panelling is still flat.
belief.loss: Four or five hundred protected buildings a year would get the standard answer instead. Either nothing happens and they burn oil until the boiler dies, or somebody dries out a 300-year-old interior with 55-degree radiators and the fabric is gone. The sector would also lose the only monitoring data anyone publishes — three conservation officers now send our figures to applicants as the reference.
belief.cause.ability: Reading a building before touching it. We put loggers in for a full heating season, do a fabric and moisture survey, and we are willing to tell a client the answer is insulation and controls rather than the heat pump they came in asking for. The engineering itself is ordinary. The discipline of surveying first and sizing honestly is what nobody else will spend the time on.
belief.cause.solution: A building that costs 60 to 70 per cent less to heat, off fossil fuel, with its fabric drier than when we started, and a monitoring record that proves it to the diocese, the insurer or whoever asks in ten years.
belief.now: Eleven people, about £1.9m turnover, booked eleven months ahead, almost entirely on referral between estates managers and conservation officers in the South West. We turn away roughly one job in three, because it is outside a day's drive or the client wants plant without the survey.
belief.aspire: The practice that sets how this work is done in Britain. Five regional teams surveying to the same standard, a published method other engineers can follow, and the fabric data from 500 buildings in one open dataset.
belief.firstStep: Write the method down properly and train a second team on it in Exeter.
belief.growthGoal: in five years, we will have taken 500 protected buildings off fossil fuel and published the fabric data from every one of them
belief.leadingPosition: we want to be known as the best in retrofitting buildings you are not allowed to change
belief.valueCost: A prep school in Wiltshire wanted to sign for a £320k plant replacement before Christmas. Our season of logging said the boiler was not the problem: the 1890 single-glazed hall was losing more than any plant could make up, and a heat pump that size would have run flat out and cost them more than the oil. We told them to spend £60k on the hall first and come back in a year. They took it to someone else, who fitted the big system. We lost the job and about £45k of margin. They rang eighteen months later with a £9k quarterly bill, asking what we had said about the hall.
belong.persona[0].story: The estates manager at a building preservation trust — six to twenty buildings on a maintenance budget set before energy prices moved. Knows the fabric intimately and has been burned by a contractor who did not. What drives them mad is being sold plant by someone who has never read a conservation management plan and treats the building as an obstacle.
belong.persona[0].location: South West England — Bristol, Bath, Somerset, Wiltshire, Dorset
belong.persona[1].story: The bursar at an independent school with Georgian or Victorian stock. Wants capital certainty, a ten-year plan and numbers that survive a governors' meeting. Driven mad by consultants' reports that cost £12k and end in 'further investigation required'.
belong.persona[1].location: South West and the Welsh Marches
belong.persona[2].story: A churchwarden or village hall committee chair. A volunteer, often retired, spending other people's money with a faculty process to satisfy and no technical background. What they actually want is to not be the person who ruined the church. Driven mad by quotes they cannot compare and jargon that makes them feel stupid.
belong.failedAlternatives: They ring a national contractor or a heat pump installer off the grant list, get a like-for-like replacement quote in a week, and nobody surveys the fabric. It fails in one of three ways: planning or the faculty refuses it; the system is sized for a leaky building, so it runs at full flow temperature and costs more than the oil did; or it works and the interior dries out and cracks. The other common route is a conservation architect who writes a lovely report that stops short of a design anyone can build.
belong.customerQuote: You are the first people who came and sat in the building for a season before telling us what to do. Your quote was higher and our bill is a third of what it was.
belong.innerCircle.wellbeing: My partner Jo, and the Wednesday swim at the lido
belong.innerCircle.direction: Hal Winters, my old boss — still the best services engineer I know
belong.innerCircle.visibility: The conservation officers who recommend us, and the SPAB technical panel
belong.innerCircle.accountability: Priya, our operations manager, who makes me quote properly
belong.innerCircle.grounding: The site team. They tell me when a drawing is fantasy.
belong.lineOfCircle: We will not design plant for a building we have not surveyed through a heating season, and we will not sign off a system we think will dry out historic fabric, however badly the client wants the grant deadline met. We have also stopped taking new-build work, even though it pays better, because it pulls the team off the thing we are actually good at.
belong.uniqueReason: Because we survey before we specify, and we will tell you not to buy the thing you came in for. Everyone else sells the plant they stock.
belong.buyer.role: A bursar, a trust board chair or a churchwarden — someone signing off capital on behalf of people who will use the building for decades
belong.buyer.risk: Their own standing. It is a six or seven-figure decision about a building people are sentimental about, taken in public: a governors' meeting, a PCC, a trustees' AGM. If the plaster cracks or the bills go up, their name is on the minutes. Most of them care more about not being the person who got it wrong than about the payback period.
best.ladder.offer: season-long fabric and moisture survey, then a designed and installed low-carbon heating system
best.ladder.problem: being stuck between a dying oil boiler and a protected interior you are not allowed to damage
best.ladder.audience: the people who look after Britain's listed and historic buildings
best.ladder.method: a full heating season of monitoring before anything is specified, and plant sized to the building we actually measured
best.ladder.result: 60 to 70 per cent off the heating bill, off fossil fuel, with the fabric drier than we found it
best.ladder.timeframe: eighteen months from first survey to commissioned system
best.usp: we're the only ones who will log your building for a season and then tell you not to buy a heat pump
best.villain: The standard answer. A whole industry that sizes plant off a spreadsheet and a postcode, grant deadlines that reward speed over survey, and a consent process so slow that clients take the quick quote out of exhaustion. What we are fighting is haste dressed up as decarbonisation.
best.failureStory: On a sixteenth-century manor in Dorset we trusted the client's own logger data instead of installing ours, because the deadline was tight. The data came from the one wing with new windows. We specified a system 40 per cent larger than the building needed and it short-cycled through the first winter. We went back, re-logged the whole house at our own cost, swapped the unit and rebalanced it — about £28k of our money. Nobody now specifies off data we did not gather, and that rule is written into the contract.
best.victory: The boiler is gone, the bills are a third, the plaster is flat, and nobody has to think about it again for twenty years.
best.competitor[0].name: Halewood M&E
best.competitor[0].strengths: Scale, in-house teams, can start next month and finance it
best.competitor[0].weaknesses: Treats a listed building like a new-build shell — no fabric survey, no moisture modelling, and their drawings get refused at faculty
best.competitor[1].name: WarmWorks Installer Network
best.competitor[1].strengths: Cheapest route to a grant, fast, and the TV advertising means everyone has heard of them
best.competitor[1].weaknesses: Franchisees on a volume model — one afternoon's survey, no interest in the building, nobody to ring in year three
best.competitor[2].name: Ashcombe Conservation Architects
best.competitor[2].strengths: Genuinely expert on fabric and respected by conservation officers; clients trust their reports
best.competitor[2].weaknesses: Stops at the report — no services design and no installation, so the client still has to find someone to build it
best.competitor[3].name: Verdantis Energy Consulting
best.competitor[3].strengths: Polished reporting, strong on grant paperwork and carbon numbers for a board
best.competitor[3].weaknesses: Never on site; the recommendations are generic and they carry no risk for whether it works
best.competitor[4].name: Rowan Heat
best.competitor[4].strengths: Local, well liked, careful installers who do good work on houses
best.competitor[4].weaknesses: Two-man band with no survey capability and no design insurance — cannot take on a school or a church
best.misconception: That we are expensive. The survey costs money up front, so our first number looks higher. What people do not see is that we are the ones who stop them spending £300k on the wrong plant.
beyond.visionBoardDetail[1]: Five hundred protected buildings off fossil fuel, with the data from every one published.
beyond.visionBoardDetail[2]: Every job cutting more carbon through fabric and controls than through new plant.
beyond.visionBoardDetail[4]: Three regional teams surveying to the same standard, and nobody leaving.
beyond.legacy: That we changed the default. In ten years I want a conservation officer to say nobody specifies plant here without a season of data any more, and that it started with Kindling — and an estates manager to say we told them the truth when it cost us the job.
beyond.giveBack: The SPAB and the local building preservation trusts. We do two surveys a year free for trusts that cannot pay, usually village halls.
beyond.accreditation: B Corp, about halfway through the assessment. We already hold ISO 9001 and the MCS and TrustMark certification the grants require.
look.palette.forbidden: The lime-green eco palette. Every grant scheme and every rival uses it and it makes us look like a leaflet. Nothing in NHS blue either.
look.admired[0].name: Patagonia
look.admired[0].why: They publish the things that make them look bad — the footprint chronicles, the repair numbers. It is the same move as us publishing moisture data. And the design is plain: the credibility comes from the evidence, not the styling.
look.admired[1].name: The National Trust
look.admired[1].why: Our clients already trust that voice. It manages to be warm and institutional at the same time, so a volunteer churchwarden and a trust board both read it as safe hands — which is exactly the two audiences we have to hold at once.
look.admired[2].name: Dishoom
look.admired[2].why: Everything is specific. The typefaces, the paper, the stories on the menu feel like they came out of one real place rather than a brand workshop. I want our reports and our vans to feel like they came from the same hands that did the survey.
look.mustKeep: The MCS and TrustMark marks, because the grants require them, ISO 9001, and the name Kindling.
